title: Why the cubes add up to a perfect square
statement: Show that $1^3 + 2^3 + 3^3 + \cdots + n^3 = \left(\dfrac{n(n+1)}{2}\right)^2$ for every positive integer $n$. Note what the right-hand side is: the square of the $n$-th triangular number.
solutionSteps: Base case. For $n = 1$ the left side is $1$, and the right side is $\left(\tfrac{1 \cdot 2}{2}\right)^2 = 1$. They agree.
Inductive hypothesis. Suppose the formula holds for some $n = k$, so $1^3 + \cdots + k^3 = \left(\tfrac{k(k+1)}{2}\right)^2$.
But $k^2 + 4k + 4 = (k+2)^2$, so this is $$\frac{(k+1)^2(k+2)^2}{4} = \left(\frac{(k+1)(k+2)}{2}\right)^2,$$ which is exactly the formula with $n = k+1$.
The base case holds and the step carries it forward, so by induction the identity holds for all $n \geq 1$.
